title: The Promotion That Went to Someone Else
script: Narrator: [measured] When the promotion I had quietly been counting on went to a colleague who'd joined two years after me, my first instinct was to assume I'd been overlooked out of pure carelessness.
Narrator: [bitter] For a week or so, I nursed a fairly ugly resentment, replaying every project I'd delivered as though the sheer effort should have spoken for itself.
Narrator: [reflective] It was only when a mentor pointed out that visibility isn't the same thing as competence that I began to question my own version of events.

Narrator: [honestly] I had, admittedly, spent years assuming solid work would simply be noticed, as though recognition arrived automatically rather than something you occasionally have to advocate for.
Narrator: [thoughtful] My colleague, meanwhile, had been routinely summarising her contributions to leadership, not out of vanity, but so her impact wasn't buried under everyone else's noise.
Narrator: [conceding] Once I admitted that, the disappointment became harder to dismiss as simple unfairness, however tempting that explanation had initially seemed.
Narrator: [determined] So instead of sulking, which frankly would have been easier, I asked my director for a candid conversation about what the next cycle would actually require of me.

Narrator: [surprised] She was refreshingly blunt, explaining I'd been perceived as reliable but somewhat invisible outside my immediate team, a description that stung precisely because it was accurate.
Narrator: [determined] Over the following months, I made a point of presenting updates myself, and speaking up in meetings I'd previously sat through in silence.
Narrator: [honestly] It felt uncomfortably self-promotional at first, as though I were performing a confidence I hadn't fully grown into.
Narrator: [reflective] Gradually, it stopped feeling like performance and started feeling like simply telling the truth about work I'd already done.
Narrator: [warmly] When the next opportunity came around, I didn't get it either, but the feedback was specific rather than vague, which told me something had genuinely shifted.
Narrator: [peacefully] I still think, had the process been more transparent, I would have wasted less energy resenting a colleague who had done nothing wrong.
Narrator: [reflective] What I've taken from it is that being overlooked isn't always evidence of injustice; sometimes it's simply evidence nobody could see what you'd never shown them.

quiz.question: What was the narrator's first reaction to being passed over for promotion?
options: She assumed she'd been overlooked out of carelessness and felt bitter resentment
quiz.explanation: She says her first instinct was to assume she'd been overlooked out of carelessness, and admits she nursed an ugly resentment.

quiz.question: What did the mentor point out to her?
options: That visibility isn't the same thing as competence
quiz.explanation: A mentor gently pointed out that visibility isn't the same thing as competence, which made her question her assumptions.

quiz.question: What had her colleague been doing differently?
options: Routinely summarising her contributions to leadership
quiz.explanation: Her colleague had been routinely summarising her contributions to leadership so her impact wasn't buried.

quiz.question: What did the director tell her when she asked for candid feedback?
options: That she was seen as reliable but somewhat invisible outside her immediate team
That she talked too much in meetings
That there were no more promotions available
quiz.explanation: The director explained she'd been perceived as reliable but somewhat invisible outside her immediate team.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude at the end?
options: Being overlooked sometimes just means nobody can see what you've never shown them
She should never speak up again
quiz.explanation: She concludes that being overlooked isn't always injustice; sometimes it's evidence nobody could see what she'd never shown them.
